KNP Mining

By: Stenette Grosskopf | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Mining anthracite coal right next to the Kruger National Park poses a huge threat to our national conservation icon, and tourism in the area...

Unique Selling Point:
Mine application MP 30/5/1/2/2/10216MR by Manzolwandle Mining (Pty) Ltd on the farms Tenbosch, Vyeboom & Turfbult approximately 93kms east of Nelspruit is sending shockwaves through the conservation community and local residents alike. The company has had prospecting rights since 2012 and it is thought that they are pushing to have the mining right approved before the prospecting rights expire. The farms border the Kruger National Park's southern border, i.e. the Crocodile River -- between Marloth Park and Ngwenya Lodge. The concerns about the mine range from the obvious ecological and hydrological impact, to the impact on business and tourism, and well as the way in which the application process has been handled.

Summary:
An unknown company called Manzolwandle Mining (Pty) Ltd is looking to mine 20Mtpa of anthracite coal right on the border of Kruger National Park. Experts are doubtful whether in fact the Northern Kangwane Coalfield can even yield such volumes. The entire area is approximately 18,000 ha. The Background Information Document (BID) submitted by Singo Consulting states that it will be open cast mining, but the EIA states that it will be a "box-cut" underground mine. Although the underground mine will be less of an eyesore than a large-scale open cast mine, the impact on the environment remains the same. Blasting will affect surrounding communities and wildlife. Increased traffic and noise pollution will spoil the sense of place -- impacting on tourism and the estimated 3,000 jobs in the hospitality industry of the area.

Two independent mining experts have pointed out various flaws with the EIA and and the Environmental Consulting Agency that conducted the EIA/EMPr. The EIA came in with a 38% plagiarism count, and the head of Singo Consulting does not have a PHD, although he claims to have one. Singo Consulting is not registered, and has never applied with EAPASA.

Further information:
The community first became aware of the mining right application in July 2018. The Marloth Park Ratepayers Ass applied for access to information in Aug 2018. They received their PAIA ref no in Oct 2018 -- to date they have received no information despite numerous follow-ups.

The process of public participation was flawed. They received the 1st notification per email on the 27th May 2019 giving them an 18 hour notice of a I & AP meeting to be held the next morning 10am. They then had another I & AP meeting at 8am Sunday 30th June 2019. Meetings were not advertised widely.

Per email, and on the background information document that was handed in at the meeting of the 30th June 2019, it states that the EIA report would be available from the 20th June 2019 at the Komatipoort Public Library until the 19th July 2019. The EIA was only made available from yesterday the 8th July 2019 which does not give a 30 day notice period as per law. They also stated that the final EIA would be made available on the 22 July 2019. This document to date is still not available. The most illegal confusing part is that the email and document stipulate that all I&AP have to be received by no later than the 19th June 2019. How can this date be valid, if documents were only made available since the 24th June and the EIA only the 8th July 2019?

All emails sent to Singo Consulting and Manzolwandle Investments to request to be registered as an interested and affected party has been returned from the 10th July 2019, stipulating that all email boxes are full. Where is the public’s right to be registered as an I & AP?.

ADDITIONAL INFORMATION:

* They aim at producing approximately 20 million tons of high-grade coal per annum. 1 ton of coal can be calculated to be in the region of 160 liters per ton (extraction) + 42 liters per ton (dust control) + 38 liters per ton (coal washing) + 229 liters per ton (evaporation) = 469 liters per ton. If upper end figures for coal washing are used, water use can rise to 581 liters per ton or more. 20 million tons x 581 liters of water = 11,62 BILLION liters of water per annum.
* The Crocodile River is oversubscribed and there is NO additional water available. The directly affected registered water users relating to this bid (in other words the land owners of the targeted mining area) is 86,017,230m3 agricultural water per annum. Currently, until we receive sufficient rainfall, ALL the irrigators abstracting from the Crocodile River are allowed 20% of their allocated water.
* WASTE MANAGEMENT PLAN - As from page 17 onwards they incorporate studies and results of Lephalale, the catchment/sub area of Moholo, Lephalala, Mogalakwena, Sand, Nzhele/Nwanedi as well as reference to Lephalale Municipality – these studies and results are for Limpopo and not Nkomazi.
* From page. 60 they state that the mining right applicant is Mafikathata Mining (PTY) Ltd with reference number LP30/5/1/2/2/10079MR where it should read Manzolwandle Investments (Pty) Ltd with reference number MP30/1/5/1/2/2/10216MR.
* TRAFFIC IMPACT ASSESSMENT - They will use Marloth Park as entry and exit between gates via Olifant Street. A typical coal truck weighs 30 tons, and Olifant Street by law only has a 9ton carrying capacity with a speed limit of 50km per hour and with wild animals constantly crossing the road as Marloth Park is highly populated with free roaming wildlife. Marloth Park is a buffer zone of the Kruger National Park.
* Marloth Park is a protected area as to conservation, as well as being a residential area and a tourist hot spot.
* The traffic count and assessments were done only on 2 days (the 23rd and 24th May 2019) and at only at 3 intersections namely: N4 and Olifant Drive (they mean Tenbosch Road), N4 and Coopersdal Road, and Olifant Drive (they mean Tenbosch Road) and the R571. This assessment was done out of peak period which is not on a public holiday, long weekend or school holidays.
* WETLAND STUDY - The wetland field study was conducted over 3 days (23rd, 24th and 25th May 2019). Site studies should ideally be conducted over differing seasons. Single-seasoned assessments such as this may potentially miss certain ecological information, thus limiting accuracy, detail and confidence. It should be noted that species of conservation concern could be present on site as suitable habitat was noted during the survey.
* SOCIAL AND LABOUR PLAN - Manzolwandle will employ over a 100 permanent employees who will represent approximately 70% of the district. Is this worth thousands of employees losing their jobs in the hospitality, tourism and agricultural sector due to the impact of a mine on our environment?
* Communities who live within the geographical area may be affected by mining activities such as river pollution by the mine’s tailings. These communities fall into 2 types namely those in existence before the mine was built and those that have developed as a result of the mining operation. (A study is underway as to establishing employment due to tourism, hospitality, agricultural sectors etc. and will be provided on completion).
* Impacts on the communities will be job loss in the tourism, hospitality and agricultural sectors, visual impact, decrease in property values, water and soil pollution, contamination, soil erosion, loss of groundwater and surface water, noise, dust, and an influx of persons (job seekers) to site which will result in an increase in opportunistic crime and put additional pressure on local government for housing and associated infrastructure.
* Employment in the above sectors have no expiration, a mine’s expectancy is 30 years or less (according to production strengths) and thereafter it leaves an environmental disaster which normally never rehabilitates.
* ECOLOGY STUDY - There are highly ecological sensitive as well as two irreplaceable Critical Biodiversity Areas (CBA) within the propose site, the northern border of the proposed site and the site is located in close proximity of the protected Kruger National Park which is across the Crocodile River. The proposed site is highly diversified in terms of flora and fauna. The site visit identified over 150 species. The irreplaceable critical biodiversity are (CBA) must be clearly marked as a “No-Go” area.
* Field surveys were conducted as to botanical, fauna (mammals and avifauna) and Herpetology (reptiles and amphibians). The following plants was found which is concerning: “Pavetta zeyheri subsp. Microlancea” (Bride’s Bush) – Rare, “Adenium swazicum” (Summer Impala Lily) – Critical (this plant is declining in its natural habitat), “Caesalpina rostrate” (beakpod plumeflower) – Vulnerable (this species is facing a high risk of extinction).
* The following Avifauna was found which is concerning: “Terathopius ecaudatus” ( Bateleur Eagle) – Endangered, “Necrosyrtes monachus” (Hooded Vulture) – Critical, “Polemaetus bellicosus” (Martial Eagle) – Endangered, “Gyps africanus” (White-backed Vulture) – Critical.
* The following Fauna was found which is concerning: “Olpogastra lugubris” (Slender Bottletail) – Vulnerable, “Crocodylus niloticus” (Nile Crocodile) – Near Threatened, “Breyiceps sopranus (Whistling Rain Frog) – Vulnerable, “Rhinolophus cohenae (Cohens’s Horseshoe Bat) – Vulnerable. Lions and Leopards (which we have in Marloth Park) are also categorized as – Vulnerable.

NB
* The source of whole chunks of the Singo report - including practically everything related to the mine design and operation originates from a LEFA Scoping report for a coal mine in the Free State compiled in 2016.
* Nkomazi Coal has a high sulphur content - should lead to serious acid formation according to Eugene Martens...

Script:


KNP MINING LINK Mine application No. MP10216MR sounds innocent enough, but it has a community in uproar, worrying about their future on the fringe of the Kruger park.

V/O The Mining Rights Application has been submitted by Manzolwandle Investments (Pty) Ltd for an area of about 18,000 ha in the Nkomazi District of the Mpumalanga Lowveld - between Malelane and Komatipoort, stretching from the border of the Kruger National Park, to about 10 kms south of the N4. Cindy Benson I'm extremely worried. It's going to be a huge impact on this environment. Number 1: we're actually a protected area. We're in the buffer zone of the Kruger National Park.

V/O Marloth Park is a 3,000ha wildlife estate that borders the Kruger National Park. Chairperson of the Ratepayers Association, Cindy Benson says the park is home to about 1,000 permanent residents, and over peak seasons the area is bustling with tourists. Cindy Benson We have got more beds in Marloth Park than what the KNP has.

V/O Together with farmers and other lodge owners in the area, they are concerned that a coal mine could change the landscape forever. Cindy Benson Who wants to come to this side of the Kruger National Park or come and visit Marloth Park if we've got all this air pollution and all these trucks.

V/O Businessman, Phillip Mkhatshwa is one of the directors of Manzolwandle Investments. Manzolwandle Derek: Basically, what are your plans for the mining area? To extract coal and not disturb the development which is there.

V/O According to Benson they first heard about the proposed mine in 2018, but then it all went quiet. Cindy Benson All of a sudden, in May, we got an 18hrs notice on email, stipulating that there would be a meeting the next morning.

V/O But Mkhatshwa says the first meeting was only really for the Mjejane community. Manzolwandle Our next meeting was supposed to go to Marloth Park, but the people of Marloth Park they just invade on that meeting.

V/O A second meeting took place on the 30th of June, but concerned Marloth residents say they got no real answers there. Mkhatshwa Derek: Apparently at one of the meetings you stated “like it or not, this mine will go ahead” Yes I did say that. You know the reason why? I know by going through compliance then we'll reach where we want to go.
V/O In its environmental management plan, the mine says it will use the main road running through Marloth Park to transport coal in 30 ton trucks. Cindy Benson We have got joggers, we have got cyclists. We have pedestrians. We have animals crossing the roads constantly.
V/O The mine’s own documents even state that a traffic impact assessment was done at three intersections in Marloth Park, but Mkhatshwa now says it's nonsense. Mkhatshwa Oh, you have been misinformed. Why do I have to go above or beyond N4, driving to Marloth Park? What for?

V/O The opencast section of the mine is earmarked for a community-owned farm about 12kms South of Marloth Park. From here they plan to mine underground, under the N4, and up to the border of Kruger. Carol I think most of the people want to come here because it's a nature reserve.

V/O Carol Nake has owned a lodge in Marloth since 2017. Carol For now we have thousands of people that are working here in Marloth park – lodges, guest houses, restaurants. V/O Along the Crocodile river to the west, lies Ngwenya Lodge – one of its directors, Paul Edkins says it draws about 12,000 visitors to the area every year. Paul Derek: Paul the mine won't be right on your doorstep, so why would it affect tourism? While they may claim that it will be 18kms away, who's to say that it won't be on our doorstep in the near future.

V/O Edkins says the Resort spends almost a third of its R50 million annual budget in the local community. That's excluding the direct tourist spending in the area. Paul You'd be looking at an average person say spending R2,500 on a trip, which is conservative. Which is around R26 million so that would be a major impact if that had to stop. Mkhatshwa Derek: This mine could threaten 9,000 people in the hospitality Industry? Look we'll add on that 9,000. If we go underground, there will be no harm around the topsoil. They won't even know there are mines where they're busy extracting coal.

V/O The mine is making promises of vast employment opportunities... Bridget They are going to employ some companies, those companies come with their employees. And also people here from Nkomazi will be employed. More than 5,000 people will be employed there. Dude The mine will bring jobs to Nkomazi.. The mine’s social and labour plan says only 150 jobs will be created once in operation... again Mkhatshwa contradicts his own reports. Manzolwandle The starting point will be 1,500 jobs that will be created there – indirect and direct. LINK This is Marloth Park's fence line with the KNP and the Crocodile river. As you can see it's desperately low and not only the animals depend on the water.

V/O Organic banana farmer Roy Plath says the sugar cane, citrus and banana farms in the area are already feeling the effects of the low water levels. Roy We get restricted every year, rationed right down. At the moment we're on about 25% rationing of our water.
V/O Plath does not believe that a mine would be in the interest of the agricultural sector here. Roy I know that every farmer is with us on this in that they don't need pollution and mining.

V/O But Mkhatshwa insists they will use only underground water, not the crocodile river, and their modern mining methods will require very little water. LINK The economy is in free-fall, almost 7 million people are unemployed. We need industry, agriculture and mining to come to the rescue but at what cost to the environment and the and our wildlife heritage? Chris: There are many many specialists who can tell you this is not a good idea. The environmental impact would be huge. First of all the ground water would be contaminated. And we haven't got enough water to begin with in this area.

V/O Dr Christine McGladdery is a research expert with a Masters in Environmental Science, and a Doctorate in International Tourism Management. Chris Another huge concern is that the people employed to do the Environmental Impact Assessment are wholly unqualified. It is full of waffle. There are no specifics. Where there are specifics, they have directly plagiarised from another report. To the extent that the entire description of the operational phase has been plagiarised right down to the number of vehicles they're going to use.

V/O As part of a mine's application, they need to appoint a company to honestly assess the impact they will have on the surrounding environment - so that the affected community can engage with the reports and give their blessing, or not. In this case, Manzolwandle appointed Singo Consulting, headed by Kenneth Singo. McGladdery studied Singo’s reports and found that they were plagiarised from other documents from completely unrelated mines. Most of the information comes from an EIA compiled in 2016 by Rock Environmental Consulting for the LEFA coal mine in the Freestate. Chris In terms of the assessment where you've got to assess the significant impacts, every single one of them is a direct copy of the LEFA colliery report.

V/O The 362 page environmental assessment is also riddled with seemingly careless mistakes. Chris For example, they're not aware that wind and rainfall actually belong under climate. We also have fauna, animals, being classified as vegetation. There is a frog that is listed as a mammal. There are scorpions which are listed as reptiles...

V/O Mr Kenneth Singo declined an on-camera interview but sent a written response stating “Part of the Desktop study is to look for information from different reports. We expect criticism and constructive comments from the stakeholders for us to make a well informed EMP. We will appreciate, constructive information, thus we can better align our standard.” He also states that “...stakeholders are hunting for errors and mistakes...” Mkhatshwa Derek: Do you think that Singo Consulting has done a thorough job with their EIA and EMP? So far to Manzolwandle we are satisfied. Derek: But are you aware that large portions of their EIA were copied and pasted from other documents? Eh, referring on EIA and other things. It's a normal thing. Derek: To copy and paste from other EIA's? No they don't copy. They refer to.

V/O On Tuesday, after our correspondence with Singo, and interview with Mkhwatshwa, Singo Consulting announced that it was withdrawing from the project...

LINK The big question about this Mining Rights application is why 18,000ha? The EIA talks about a 32ha opencast mine, south of the N4 and an underground mine ranging between 1,300 and 2,300 ha. It just doesn't add up. Mkhatshwa Usually the mining field you cannot confine yourself at a small place because when you do an opencast, there are theses topsoil which will need space. You put it away from where you are going to mine.

V/O Manzolwandle's Background Information Document states they will extract 20 million tonnes of anthracite coal a year for 30 years. Mkhatshwa negates his own figures and says it’s actually 1.5 million tonnes... Mkhatshwa Derek: Based on the paperwork people are asking questions regarding the credibility of your company. I mean do you have the technical and financial support to successfully run this operation? Yes, we do have but I won't disclose the name of my investor. Why not? Shouldn't it be public? No. That one is the confidentiality of Manzolwandle.

V/O The Mpumalanga department of Mineral Resources did not respond to our emails and curiously, the National Department of Mineral Resources wrote that they had no record of this mining application at all. As many questions remain unanswered, it seems for the residents of Marloth park the battle has just begun.... Chris: Derek: Can you summarise this report of yours in 3 sentences? Without being rude? Without that. Uhm, highly unprofessional, totally lacking substance and insulting to the people who are meant to read it, who it's made for. It's for the public participation process. So, insulting to us and insulting to the DMR ultimately as well.

Author Last Updated 18 August 2019 - Carte Blanche HD nombuso@carteblanche.co.za 18 October 2019 Script: KNP MINING LINK Mine application No. MP10216MR sounds innocent enough, but it has a community in uproar, worrying about their future on the fringe of the Kruger park. V/O The Mining Rights Application has been submitted by Manzolwandle Investments (Pty) Ltd for an area of about 18,000 ha in the Nkomazi District of the Mpumalanga Lowveld - between Malelane and Komatipoort, stretching from the border of the Kruger National Park, to about 10 kms south of the N4. Cindy Benson I'm extremely worried. It's going to be a huge impact on this environment. Number 1: we're actually a protected area. We're in the buffer zone of the Kruger National Park. V/O Marloth Park is a 3,000ha wildlife estate that borders the Kruger National Park. Chairperson of the Ratepayers Association, Cindy Benson says the park is home to about 1,000 permanent residents, and over peak seasons the area is bustling with tourists. Cindy Benson We have got more beds in Marloth Park than what the KNP has. V/O Together with farmers and other lodge owners in the area, they are concerned that a coal mine could change the landscape forever. Cindy Benson Who wants to come to this side of the Kruger National Park or come and visit Marloth Park if we've got all this air pollution and all these trucks. V/O Businessman, Phillip Mkhatshwa is one of the directors of Manzolwandle Investments. Manzolwandle Derek: Basically, what are your plans for the mining area? To extract coal and not disturb the development which is there. V/O According to Benson they first heard about the proposed mine in 2018, but then it all went quiet. Cindy Benson All of a sudden, in May, we got an 18hrs notice on email, stipulating that there would be a meeting the next morning. V/O But Mkhatshwa says the first meeting was only really for the Mjejane community. Manzolwandle Our next meeting was supposed to go to Marloth Park, but the people of Marloth Park they just invade on that meeting. V/O A second meeting took place on the 30th of June, but concerned Marloth residents say they got no real answers there. Mkhatshwa Derek: Apparently at one of the meetings you stated “like it or not, this mine will go ahead” Yes I did say that. You know the reason why? I know by going through compliance then we'll reach where we want to go. V/O In its environmental management plan, the mine says it will use the main road running through Marloth Park to transport coal in 30 ton trucks. Cindy Benson We have got joggers, we have got cyclists. We have pedestrians. We have animals crossing the roads constantly. V/O The mine’s own documents even state that a traffic impact assessment was done at three intersections in Marloth Park, but Mkhatshwa now says it's nonsense. Mkhatshwa Oh, you have been misinformed. Why do I have to go above or beyond N4, driving to Marloth Park? What for? V/O The opencast section of the mine is earmarked for a community-owned farm about 12kms South of Marloth Park. From here they plan to mine underground, under the N4, and up to the border of Kruger. Carol I think most of the people want to come here because it's a nature reserve. V/O Carol Nake has owned a lodge in Marloth since 2017. Carol For now we have thousands of people that are working here in Marloth park – lodges, guest houses, restaurants. V/O Along the Crocodile river to the west, lies Ngwenya Lodge – one of its directors, Paul Edkins says it draws about 12,000 visitors to the area every year. Paul Derek: Paul the mine won't be right on your doorstep, so why would it affect tourism? While they may claim that it will be 18kms away, who's to say that it won't be on our doorstep in the near future. V/O Edkins says the Resort spends almost a third of its R50 million annual budget in the local community. That's excluding the direct tourist spending in the area. Paul You'd be looking at an average person say spending R2,500 on a trip, which is conservative. Which is around R26 million so that would be a major impact if that had to stop. Mkhatshwa Derek: This mine could threaten 9,000 people in the hospitality Industry? Look we'll add on that 9,000. If we go underground, there will be no harm around the topsoil. They won't even know there are mines where they're busy extracting coal. V/O The mine is making promises of vast employment opportunities... Bridget They are going to employ some companies, those companies come with their employees. And also people here from Nkomazi will be employed. More than 5,000 people will be employed there. Dude The mine will bring jobs to Nkomazi.. The mine’s social and labour plan says only 150 jobs will be created once in operation... again Mkhatshwa contradicts his own reports. Manzolwandle The starting point will be 1,500 jobs that will be created there – indirect and direct. LINK This is Marloth Park's fence line with the KNP and the Crocodile river. As you can see it's desperately low and not only the animals depend on the water. V/O Organic banana farmer Roy Plath says the sugar cane, citrus and banana farms in the area are already feeling the effects of the low water levels. Roy We get restricted every year, rationed right down. At the moment we're on about 25% rationing of our water. V/O Plath does not believe that a mine would be in the interest of the agricultural sector here. Roy I know that every farmer is with us on this in that they don't need pollution and mining. V/O But Mkhatshwa insists they will use only underground water, not the crocodile river, and their modern mining methods will require very little water. LINK The economy is in free-fall, almost 7 million people are unemployed. We need industry, agriculture and mining to come to the rescue but at what cost to the environment and the and our wildlife heritage? Chris: There are many many specialists who can tell you this is not a good idea. The environmental impact would be huge. First of all the ground water would be contaminated. And we haven't got enough water to begin with in this area. V/O Dr Christine McGladdery is a research expert with a Masters in Environmental Science, and a Doctorate in International Tourism Management. Chris Another huge concern is that the people employed to do the Environmental Impact Assessment are wholly unqualified. It is full of waffle. There are no specifics. Where there are specifics, they have directly plagiarised from another report. To the extent that the entire description of the operational phase has been plagiarised right down to the number of vehicles they're going to use. V/O As part of a mine's application, they need to appoint a company to honestly assess the impact they will have on the surrounding environment - so that the affected community can engage with the reports and give their blessing, or not. In this case, Manzolwandle appointed Singo Consulting, headed by Kenneth Singo. McGladdery studied Singo’s reports and found that they were plagiarised from other documents from completely unrelated mines. Most of the information comes from an EIA compiled in 2016 by Rock Environmental Consulting for the LEFA coal mine in the Freestate. Chris In terms of the assessment where you've got to assess the significant impacts, every single one of them is a direct copy of the LEFA colliery report. V/O The 362 page environmental assessment is also riddled with seemingly careless mistakes. Chris For example, they're not aware that wind and rainfall actually belong under climate. We also have fauna, animals, being classified as vegetation. There is a frog that is listed as a mammal. There are scorpions which are listed as reptiles... V/O Mr Kenneth Singo declined an on-camera interview but sent a written response stating “Part of the Desktop study is to look for information from different reports. We expect criticism and constructive comments from the stakeholders for us to make a well informed EMP. We will appreciate, constructive information, thus we can better align our standard.” He also states that “...stakeholders are hunting for errors and mistakes...” Mkhatshwa Derek: Do you think that Singo Consulting has done a thorough job with their EIA and EMP? So far to Manzolwandle we are satisfied. Derek: But are you aware that large portions of their EIA were copied and pasted from other documents? Eh, referring on EIA and other things. It's a normal thing. Derek: To copy and paste from other EIA's? No they don't copy. They refer to. V/O On Tuesday, after our correspondence with Singo, and interview with Mkhwatshwa, Singo Consulting announced that it was withdrawing from the project... LINK The big question about this Mining Rights application is why 18,000ha? The EIA talks about a 32ha opencast mine, south of the N4 and an underground mine ranging between 1,300 and 2,300 ha. It just doesn't add up. Mkhatshwa Usually the mining field you cannot confine yourself at a small place because when you do an opencast, there are theses topsoil which will need space. You put it away from where you are going to mine. V/O Manzolwandle's Background Information Document states they will extract 20 million tonnes of anthracite coal a year for 30 years. Mkhatshwa negates his own figures and says it’s actually 1.5 million tonnes... Mkhatshwa Derek: Based on the paperwork people are asking questions regarding the credibility of your company. I mean do you have the technical and financial support to successfully run this operation? Yes, we do have but I won't disclose the name of my investor. Why not? Shouldn't it be public? No. That one is the confidentiality of Manzolwandle. V/O The Mpumalanga department of Mineral Resources did not respond to our emails and curiously, the National Department of Mineral Resources wrote that they had no record of this mining application at all. As many questions remain unanswered, it seems for the residents of Marloth park the battle has just begun.... Chris: Derek: Can you summarise this report of yours in 3 sentences? Without being rude? Without that. Uhm, highly unprofessional, totally lacking substance and insulting to the people who are meant to read it, who it's made for. It's for the public participation process. So, insulting to us and insulting to the DMR ultimately as well.

metadata.Unique Selling Point: Mine application MP 30/5/1/2/2/10216MR by Manzolwandle Mining (Pty) Ltd on the farms Tenbosch, Vyeboom & Turfbult approximately 93kms east of Nelspruit is sending shockwaves through the conservation community and local residents alike. The company has had prospecting rights since 2012 and it is thought that they are pushing to have the mining right approved before the prospecting rights expire. The farms border the Kruger National Park's southern border, i.e. the Crocodile River -- between Marloth Park and Ngwenya Lodge. The concerns about the mine range from the obvious ecological and hydrological impact, to the impact on business and tourism, and well as the way in which the application process has been handled.
metadata.Summary: An unknown company called Manzolwandle Mining (Pty) Ltd is looking to mine 20Mtpa of anthracite coal right on the border of Kruger National Park. Experts are doubtful whether in fact the Northern Kangwane Coalfield can even yield such volumes. The entire area is approximately 18,000 ha. The Background Information Document (BID) submitted by Singo Consulting states that it will be open cast mining, but the EIA states that it will be a "box-cut" underground mine. Although the underground mine will be less of an eyesore than a large-scale open cast mine, the impact on the environment remains the same. Blasting will affect surrounding communities and wildlife. Increased traffic and noise pollution will spoil the sense of place -- impacting on tourism and the estimated 3,000 jobs in the hospitality industry of the area. Two independent mining experts have pointed out various flaws with the EIA and and the Environmental Consulting Agency that conducted the EIA/EMPr. The EIA came in with a 38% plagiarism count, and the head of Singo Consulting does not have a PHD, although he claims to have one. Singo Consulting is not registered, and has never applied with EAPASA.
metadata.Further information: The community first became aware of the mining right application in July 2018. The Marloth Park Ratepayers Ass applied for access to information in Aug 2018. They received their PAIA ref no in Oct 2018 -- to date they have received no information despite numerous follow-ups. The process of public participation was flawed. They received the 1st notification per email on the 27th May 2019 giving them an 18 hour notice of a I & AP meeting to be held the next morning 10am. They then had another I & AP meeting at 8am Sunday 30th June 2019. Meetings were not advertised widely. Per email, and on the background information document that was handed in at the meeting of the 30th June 2019, it states that the EIA report would be available from the 20th June 2019 at the Komatipoort Public Library until the 19th July 2019. The EIA was only made available from yesterday the 8th July 2019 which does not give a 30 day notice period as per law. They also stated that the final EIA would be made available on the 22 July 2019. This document to date is still not available. The most illegal confusing part is that the email and document stipulate that all I&AP have to be received by no later than the 19th June 2019. How can this date be valid, if documents were only made available since the 24th June and the EIA only the 8th July 2019? All emails sent to Singo Consulting and Manzolwandle Investments to request to be registered as an interested and affected party has been returned from the 10th July 2019, stipulating that all email boxes are full. Where is the public’s right to be registered as an I & AP?. ADDITIONAL INFORMATION: * They aim at producing approximately 20 million tons of high-grade coal per annum. 1 ton of coal can be calculated to be in the region of 160 liters per ton (extraction) + 42 liters per ton (dust control) + 38 liters per ton (coal washing) + 229 liters per ton (evaporation) = 469 liters per ton. If upper end figures for coal washing are used, water use can rise to 581 liters per ton or more. 20 million tons x 581 liters of water = 11,62 BILLION liters of water per annum. * The Crocodile River is oversubscribed and there is NO additional water available. The directly affected registered water users relating to this bid (in other words the land owners of the targeted mining area) is 86,017,230m3 agricultural water per annum. Currently, until we receive sufficient rainfall, ALL the irrigators abstracting from the Crocodile River are allowed 20% of their allocated water. * WASTE MANAGEMENT PLAN - As from page 17 onwards they incorporate studies and results of Lephalale, the catchment/sub area of Moholo, Lephalala, Mogalakwena, Sand, Nzhele/Nwanedi as well as reference to Lephalale Municipality – these studies and results are for Limpopo and not Nkomazi. * From page. 60 they state that the mining right applicant is Mafikathata Mining (PTY) Ltd with reference number LP30/5/1/2/2/10079MR where it should read Manzolwandle Investments (Pty) Ltd with reference number MP30/1/5/1/2/2/10216MR. * TRAFFIC IMPACT ASSESSMENT - They will use Marloth Park as entry and exit between gates via Olifant Street. A typical coal truck weighs 30 tons, and Olifant Street by law only has a 9ton carrying capacity with a speed limit of 50km per hour and with wild animals constantly crossing the road as Marloth Park is highly populated with free roaming wildlife. Marloth Park is a buffer zone of the Kruger National Park. * Marloth Park is a protected area as to conservation, as well as being a residential area and a tourist hot spot. * The traffic count and assessments were done only on 2 days (the 23rd and 24th May 2019) and at only at 3 intersections namely: N4 and Olifant Drive (they mean Tenbosch Road), N4 and Coopersdal Road, and Olifant Drive (they mean Tenbosch Road) and the R571. This assessment was done out of peak period which is not on a public holiday, long weekend or school holidays. * WETLAND STUDY - The wetland field study was conducted over 3 days (23rd, 24th and 25th May 2019). Site studies should ideally be conducted over differing seasons. Single-seasoned assessments such as this may potentially miss certain ecological information, thus limiting accuracy, detail and confidence. It should be noted that species of conservation concern could be present on site as suitable habitat was noted during the survey. * SOCIAL AND LABOUR PLAN - Manzolwandle will employ over a 100 permanent employees who will represent approximately 70% of the district. Is this worth thousands of employees losing their jobs in the hospitality, tourism and agricultural sector due to the impact of a mine on our environment? * Communities who live within the geographical area may be affected by mining activities such as river pollution by the mine’s tailings. These communities fall into 2 types namely those in existence before the mine was built and those that have developed as a result of the mining operation. (A study is underway as to establishing employment due to tourism, hospitality, agricultural sectors etc. and will be provided on completion). * Impacts on the communities will be job loss in the tourism, hospitality and agricultural sectors, visual impact, decrease in property values, water and soil pollution, contamination, soil erosion, loss of groundwater and surface water, noise, dust, and an influx of persons (job seekers) to site which will result in an increase in opportunistic crime and put additional pressure on local government for housing and associated infrastructure. * Employment in the above sectors have no expiration, a mine’s expectancy is 30 years or less (according to production strengths) and thereafter it leaves an environmental disaster which normally never rehabilitates. * ECOLOGY STUDY - There are highly ecological sensitive as well as two irreplaceable Critical Biodiversity Areas (CBA) within the propose site, the northern border of the proposed site and the site is located in close proximity of the protected Kruger National Park which is across the Crocodile River. The proposed site is highly diversified in terms of flora and fauna. The site visit identified over 150 species. The irreplaceable critical biodiversity are (CBA) must be clearly marked as a “No-Go” area. * Field surveys were conducted as to botanical, fauna (mammals and avifauna) and Herpetology (reptiles and amphibians). The following plants was found which is concerning: “Pavetta zeyheri subsp. Microlancea” (Bride’s Bush) – Rare, “Adenium swazicum” (Summer Impala Lily) – Critical (this plant is declining in its natural habitat), “Caesalpina rostrate” (beakpod plumeflower) – Vulnerable (this species is facing a high risk of extinction). * The following Avifauna was found which is concerning: “Terathopius ecaudatus” ( Bateleur Eagle) – Endangered, “Necrosyrtes monachus” (Hooded Vulture) – Critical, “Polemaetus bellicosus” (Martial Eagle) – Endangered, “Gyps africanus” (White-backed Vulture) – Critical. * The following Fauna was found which is concerning: “Olpogastra lugubris” (Slender Bottletail) – Vulnerable, “Crocodylus niloticus” (Nile Crocodile) – Near Threatened, “Breyiceps sopranus (Whistling Rain Frog) – Vulnerable, “Rhinolophus cohenae (Cohens’s Horseshoe Bat) – Vulnerable. Lions and Leopards (which we have in Marloth Park) are also categorized as – Vulnerable. NB * The source of whole chunks of the Singo report - including practically everything related to the mine design and operation originates from a LEFA Scoping report for a coal mine in the Free State compiled in 2016. * Nkomazi Coal has a high sulphur content - should lead to serious acid formation according to Eugene Martens...
